'''The  1985–86 season''' was the 87th completed season of [[English Football League|The Football League]].

==Final league tables and results ==
The tables and results below are reproduced here in the exact form that they can be found at The Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation website,<ref name="rsssf">{{cite web|url=https://www.rsssf.org/engpaul/FLA/1985-86.html |title=England 1985–86 |publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation |access-date=24 February 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100127100741/http://www.rsssf.com/engpaul/FLA/1985-86.html |archive-date=27 January 2010 |url-status=live }}</ref> with home and away statistics separated.

During the first five seasons of the league, that is, until the season 1893–94, re-election process concerned the clubs which finished in the bottom four of the league. From the 1894–95 season and until the 1920–21 season the re-election process was required of the clubs which finished in the bottom three of the league. From the 1922–23 season on it was required of the bottom two teams of both Third Division North and Third Division South. Since the [[Football League Fourth Division|Fourth Division]] was established in the [[1958–59 Football League|1958–59 season]], the re-election process has concerned the bottom four clubs in that division.<ref>Ian Laschke: ''Rothmans Book of Football League Records 1888–89 to 1978–79''. Macdonald and Jane’s, London & Sydney, 1980.</ref>

In a close three-horse race, [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] pipped [[Everton F.C.|Everton]] and [[West Ham United F.C.|West Ham United]] to the [[Football League First Division|First Division]] title,<ref name="independent 1985 blackout">[https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/news-and-comment/remember-the-1985-tv-blackout-only-the-big-yin-knew-who-mcavennie-was-2052962.html Remember the 1985 TV blackout? Only the Big Yin knew who McAvennie was], Simon Hart, The Independent, 22 October 2011</ref> while also defeating Merseyside rivals Everton in the [[1985–86 FA Cup#Final|FA Cup Final]], thereby completing a historic double. [[Manchester United F.C.|Manchester United]] had been ten points clear in early November after [[1985–86 Manchester United F.C. season|winning their first ten matches; and thirteen of their first fifteen]],<ref name=tv1985>[https://www.theguardian.com/football/that-1980s-sports-blog/2019/dec/03/football-fans-christmas-watching-live-game-tv When football fans did not see a single match on TV over Christmas], Steven Pye, The Guardian, 3 December 2019</ref> but injuries, loss of form and ineffective signings had seen them fall away, leaving them still waiting for their first league title since [[1966–67 in English football|1967]], mounting the pressure of manager [[Ron Atkinson]], although the [[Old Trafford]] board initially decided to stick with Atkinson as their manager for the following season.

[[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] finished seventh in the league for a third successive season, their manager [[Don Howe]] resigning a few weeks before the end of the season after it was reported that [[Terry Venables]] had been offered his job. Coach [[Steve Burtenshaw]] was placed in temporary charge of the first team until the end of the season, when [[George Graham (footballer, born 1944)|George Graham]] returned to [[Arsenal Stadium|Highbury]] as manager. [[Tottenham Hotspur F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]] finished a disappointing 10th in the league, prompting the [[White Hart Lane]] board to sack manager [[Peter Shreeves]] and replace him with [[Luton Town F.C.|Luton Town's]] [[David Pleat]].

At the lower end of the table, a disastrous season saw [[West Bromwich Albion F.C.|West Bromwich Albion]] relegated in bottom place after just four wins in the league, while nearby rivals [[Birmingham City F.C.|Birmingham City]] fared nearly as badly, and were relegated in second place from bottom; both clubs would not return to the top flight until 2002. Their local rivals [[Aston Villa F.C.|Aston Villa]] nearly went down with them, before a late upturn in form secured their survival. [[Oxford United F.C.|Oxford United]] had a memorable first season at this level as League Cup winners, but spent much of the season battling against relegation before finally managing to beat the drop. The final relegation place went to [[Ipswich Town F.C.|Ipswich Town]], who had gradually fallen out of contention with the First Division's leading pack since [[Bobby Robson]]'s departure to manage the England team four years earlier.

==Election/Re-election to the Football League==
As champions of the [[National League (English football)|Alliance Premier League]], [[Enfield F.C.|Enfield]] won the right to apply for election to the Football League, to replace one of the four bottom teams in the 1985–86 Football League Fourth Division. The vote went as follows:

{| class="wikitable" style="text-align:left;"
!width=140| Club
!width=185| Final Position
!width=50| Votes
|-
| [[Exeter City F.C.|Exeter City]] || 21st (Fourth Division) || align=center|64
|-
| [[Preston North End F.C.|Preston North End]] || 23rd (Fourth Division) || align=center|62.5
|-
| [[Cambridge United F.C.|Cambridge United]] || 22nd (Fourth Division) || align=center|61
|-
| [[Torquay United F.C.|Torquay United]] || 24th (Fourth Division) || align=center|61
|-
| [[Enfield F.C.|Enfield]] || 1st (Alliance Premier League) || align=center|7.5
|}

Hence, all four Football League teams were re-elected, and Enfield were denied membership of the Football League.

This was the last season in which the Alliance Premier League champions had to apply for election to the Football League. From the 1986–87 season, when the Alliance Premier League was re-branded as the Football Conference, the champions were automatically promoted, provided that they met the criteria set by the Football League.
